title: African and Latin American Philosophy
subtitle: Persons through persons, truth as rootedness, and philosophy from the underside of history
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain ubuntu and the debate between radical and moderate communitarian accounts of personhood
By the end you will be able to describe Kwasi Wiredu's programme of conceptual decolonization and Odera Oruka's sage philosophy, and why they rejected 'ethnophilosophy'
By the end you will be able to outline James Maffie's reconstruction of Aztec (Nahua) metaphysics and epistemology, including teotl and neltiliztli
By the end you will be able to state Enrique Dussel's critique of modernity and the core claims of the philosophy of liberation
hook:
Imagine asking a philosopher what a person is, and receiving the answer: not yet. Not a person *yet*, because personhood is something you grow into through how you live among others, the way someone becomes a friend or an elder. To many modern Western ears this sounds alarming. Surely a person is a person from birth, by virtue of reason or consciousness or a soul? Yet this idea, that personhood is achieved in community, sits at the heart of an important strand of African philosophy, and it raises questions that individualist traditions find hard even to ask.

This lesson travels across two continents. It is not one tradition but several, and the greatest danger is to lump them together as 'non-Western' as though they shared anything simply by not being European. On Day 86 you met decolonial thought, and on Day 87 the ubuntu ethic. Here we go deeper: into the twentieth-century debate about what African philosophy even *is*, into Ghanaian, Kenyan and Nigerian philosophers who answered it, into the metaphysics of the Nahua (Aztec) world reconstructed from colonial-era sources, and into Enrique Dussel's challenge to the story modern Europe told about itself.

sections.heading: What Is African Philosophy? A Debate About the Question
sections.body:
In 1945 the Belgian missionary Placide Tempels published *Bantu Philosophy*, arguing that the Bantu-speaking peoples of the Congo shared an implicit philosophy centred on 'vital force'. It was meant sympathetically, as a rebuttal to colonial claims that Africans lacked rational thought. But it sparked a fierce reaction from African philosophers.

The Beninese philosopher **Paulin Hountondji**, in *African Philosophy: Myth and Reality* (1976), coined a critical label: **ethnophilosophy**. This is the practice of reconstructing a supposedly unanimous worldview of a whole people from their proverbs, myths and customs, and calling it their philosophy. Hountondji objected that it treats Africans as collectively holding one view, which he called **unanimism**, when real philosophy involves individual thinkers who argue, disagree and criticise their own traditions. It also assumes that African thought is frozen in a traditional past.

The Kenyan philosopher **Henry Odera Oruka** (1944–1995) agreed that ethnophilosophy was inadequate, but thought Hountondji went too far in implying that only academic, written philosophy counts. Oruka identified several trends in African philosophy: ethnophilosophy; **nationalist-ideological** philosophy (the political thought of leaders like Julius Nyerere and Kwame Nkrumah); **professional** philosophy (academic work by trained philosophers); and his own project, **philosophic sagacity**.

In the 1970s and 1980s Oruka and his team interviewed elders in rural Kenya, recording their views on God, death, justice, gender and the good life. He distinguished the **folk sage**, who knows and transmits the received wisdom of the community, from the **philosophic sage**, who reflects critically on that wisdom, and sometimes rejects it, giving reasons. His sages included people with no formal schooling who argued, for example, against beliefs in witchcraft or against particular customs. Oruka's point was that critical, individual reflection did not arrive in Africa with universities or writing. Think of Socrates (Day 9), who also wrote nothing. The method was criticised too: how much of the 'philosophy' comes from the interviewer's questions? Oruka acknowledged the collaboration, calling the resulting dialogues joint products.

sections.heading: Ubuntu and the Achievement of Personhood
sections.body:
**Ubuntu** is a word from the Nguni languages of southern Africa (including isiZulu and isiXhosa). It is usually explained through the maxim *umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu*: a person is a person through other persons. The Kenyan-born theologian **John Mbiti** gave a widely quoted formulation in *African Religions and Philosophy* (1969): I am because we are; and since we are, therefore I am. Notice the deliberate contrast with Descartes's 'I think, therefore I am' (Day 43). For Descartes, the self is known first and alone; others are an inference. For ubuntu, the self is constituted by its relations.

The Nigerian philosopher **Ifeanyi Menkiti**, in an influential 1984 essay, 'Person and Community in African Traditional Thought', drew a bold conclusion. In much African thought, he argued, personhood is **processual** and **normative**: one becomes a person through moral development and participation in community. Children are not yet fully persons in this thick sense; elders, having lived well, are persons in the fullest sense, and the ancestors continue to have standing after death. Personhood, on this view, is something at which one can fail.

The Ghanaian philosopher **Kwame Gyekye** (1939–2019) objected. Menkiti's **radical communitarianism**, he argued, risks denying individuals any rights or standing that the community has not conferred, and so makes it impossible to criticise the community. Gyekye defended **moderate communitarianism**: humans are naturally relational, and community shapes us profoundly, but each person also has intrinsic worth, a capacity for rational choice, and rights that the community must respect. He pointed to Akan proverbs that celebrate individuality as well as belonging.

The South African-based philosopher **Thaddeus Metz** has tried to state ubuntu as a precise moral theory rivalling utilitarianism and Kantianism: an action is right, roughly, insofar as it respects or promotes **harmonious relationships**, understood as sharing a way of life (identity) and caring for one another's quality of life (solidarity). On this view, what is wrong with lying or stealing is not that it reduces total welfare or violates a rational rule, but that it treats someone in an unfriendly, divisive way. Critics question whether one theory can capture the variety of African moral thought. But the debate shows ubuntu being developed with the same rigour as any Western ethical theory.

sections.heading: Kwasi Wiredu and Conceptual Decolonization
sections.body:
The Ghanaian philosopher **Kwasi Wiredu** (1931–2022), trained at Oxford in the analytic tradition, offered one of the most original programmes in modern African philosophy. In *Philosophy and an African Culture* (1980) and later essays collected in *Cultural Universals and Particulars* (1996), he argued for **conceptual decolonization**: African philosophers should examine the concepts they absorbed through colonial education, in English or French, and ask whether the problems those concepts generate make sense when thought through in an African language.

His most famous test case concerns Descartes. In Wiredu's own language, Akan, he argued, existence is expressed as *wo ho*, 'to be there', at some place. So 'I think, therefore I am' becomes something like 'I think, therefore I am there, somewhere', which loses its force: it can no longer express the existence of a mind that is nowhere. Similarly, he argued that the Cartesian idea of an immaterial, non-spatial substance is hard to formulate in Akan, which suggests that the mind-body problem may be partly an artefact of a particular philosophical vocabulary. Wiredu did not conclude that Akan is better or that Western philosophy is wrong, but that concepts must be tested, not inherited.

He applied the same critical spirit to his own tradition. He argued that traditional beliefs should be held to the same standards of evidence as any others, criticising what he saw as authoritarianism and unscientific beliefs in some customary thought, just as one would in European folk traditions.

In political philosophy, Wiredu drew on the traditional councils of the Ashanti, where decisions were reached by extended discussion aiming at **consensus** rather than majority vote. He proposed a **non-party consensual democracy** for modern African states, arguing that majoritarian multi-party systems imported from Europe often produced winner-takes-all ethnic conflict. Critics replied that consensus can mask pressure on dissenters to conform, and that the old councils were not open to everyone. The proposal remains debated.

sections.heading: Aztec Philosophy: A World in Motion
sections.body:
Before 1521, the Nahuatl-speaking peoples of central Mexico, among them the Mexica of Tenochtitlan whom we call Aztecs, had specialists called **tlamatinime**, 'knowers of things', who reflected on reality, knowledge and the good life. What we know comes largely through sources compiled after the Spanish conquest, especially the *Florentine Codex*, assembled by the Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún with Nahua collaborators in the sixteenth century. These sources are filtered through colonial and Christian purposes, so reconstruction requires care. The Mexican historian **Miguel León-Portilla** pioneered the study of Nahua thought in *Aztec Thought and Culture* (Spanish 1956).

The philosopher **James Maffie**, in *Aztec Philosophy: Understanding a World in Motion* (2014), offers the most systematic modern reconstruction. On his reading, Nahua metaphysics is a **process monism**. There is one sacred reality, **teotl**, which is not a being or a god in the Western sense but a continually self-generating, self-transforming energy. Everything that exists is an aspect or moment of teotl's ceaseless motion. Recall Heraclitus's flux (Day 4) and the Daoist Way in lesson 2; there are real resonances, but Maffie insists Nahua thought be understood on its own terms.

Maffie identifies three patterns of motion through which teotl works: **olin**, curving, oscillating, bouncing motion, as in the rhythms of the heartbeat, breathing and the sun's path; **malinalli**, twisting and spinning, as in spinning fibre into thread, through which energy is transmitted; and **nepantla**, weaving, middling, the in-between motion of things mutually interwoven, as threads in cloth. The cosmos is less a collection of things than a vast weaving.

This changes epistemology. In Nahua thought, Maffie argues, truth is not chiefly correspondence between a statement and a fact (the dominant Western picture), but **neltiliztli**: well-rootedness, authenticity, being genuinely grounded in teotl. A person, a song or an action can be 'true' in this sense, as a tree is well-rooted. The Nahua said that the earth is slippery (a saying recorded in the *Florentine Codex*): life is a precarious path on which it is easy to lose one's balance. Ethics, on this view, is the practical art of keeping one's footing, finding balance and moderation in a world that never stops moving. The philosopher Sebastian Purcell has compared this to Aristotle's mean (Day 20), while noting that the goal is a rooted life rather than individual eudaimonia.

sections.heading: Enrique Dussel and the Philosophy of Liberation
sections.body:
In Latin America, a long-running debate asked whether there could be an authentic Latin American philosophy, or only imitations of European fashions. The Peruvian philosopher Augusto Salazar Bondy argued in 1968 that philosophy in a dependent, colonised society would itself be dependent until the society was liberated. The Mexican Leopoldo Zea replied that Latin Americans had always philosophised, precisely about their own circumstances.

**Enrique Dussel** (1934–2023), born in Argentina and exiled to Mexico in 1975 after a bomb attack on his home, became the leading figure of the **philosophy of liberation**, which developed alongside the liberation theology of Gustavo Gutiérrez. His *Philosophy of Liberation* (1977) begins from the perspective of the **victim**: the poor, the colonised, the excluded.

Dussel's best-known thesis is about the birth of modernity. The standard European story locates modernity in the Renaissance, the Reformation and Descartes. Dussel argues that modernity began in **1492**, when Europe encountered, conquered and exploited the Americas, which provided the wealth and the sense of world-centrality on which European self-confidence grew. Before Descartes's *ego cogito*, 'I think', there was the *ego conquiro*, 'I conquer'. The European subject understood itself as the centre of the world partly because it had made others into its periphery. Dussel calls the self-flattering European story the **myth of modernity**: it presents Europe as developing from its own internal resources, and then justifies violence against others as the price of bringing them civilisation.

Drawing on Emmanuel Levinas, Dussel speaks of **exteriority**: the Other who stands outside the dominant system (the 'totality'), whose face makes an ethical demand the system cannot hear. Liberation philosophy begins by listening to that demand. Dussel does not reject modernity's achievements; he proposes **transmodernity**, a future built by the many cultures that modernity marginalised, in dialogue rather than under one centre.

Critics argue that Dussel's sweeping narrative underplays the internal sources of European modernity and treats 'Europe' and 'the periphery' as more uniform than they were. Defenders reply that the point is not to deny the Renaissance but to refuse to tell its story without the Atlantic.

sections.heading: Beyond 'Non-Western': Learning Without Flattening
sections.body:
What do these traditions share? Less than a simple label suggests. Akan and Nguni thought differ from each other, as Nahua thought differs from the liberation philosophy written in Mexico City five centuries later. But several themes recur, and they press on assumptions the main course mostly took for granted.

First, **relational selves**. Ubuntu's 'person through persons' and the Nahua weaving of nepantla both resist the picture of the self as an isolated mind, a picture the Western tradition itself challenged through Hegel (Day 59), care ethics (Day 85) and the Buddhist ideas of lesson 3.

Second, **process over substance**. Teotl, like the Dao, privileges motion and relation over fixed things, reopening the ancient debate between Heraclitus and Parmenides.

Third, **philosophy and power**. Hountondji, Wiredu and Dussel all ask who gets counted as a philosopher, in which language, and whose experience defines the questions. That is not a rejection of argument; it is an argument about the conditions of argument. Miranda Fricker's idea of **epistemic injustice** (Day 86) gives one name to the harm involved: being wronged in your capacity as a knower.

The lesson for comparative philosophy is double. We should not romanticise traditions as wise simply because they are old or marginalised: Wiredu and Oruka's sages criticised their own cultures, and so should we. Nor should we translate them into familiar Western boxes, calling ubuntu 'just communitarianism' or teotl 'just pantheism'. Respect means taking them seriously as claims that might be true, and therefore as claims that might be argued with.

keyQuote.text: I am because we are; and since we are, therefore I am.
keyQuote.source: John S. Mbiti, African Religions and Philosophy (1969)

modernConnection.title: Ubuntu in Courtrooms and in AI Ethics
modernConnection.body:
Ubuntu has shaped real institutions. In 1995, in *S v Makwanyane*, South Africa's new Constitutional Court abolished the death penalty, and several judges appealed to ubuntu: a society committed to the dignity of every person, including offenders, cannot extinguish a life as punishment. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996–1998), chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, offered amnesty to perpetrators of apartheid-era abuses who made full public disclosure, and invited victims to tell their stories. Tutu defended this in *No Future Without Forgiveness* (1999) as an expression of ubuntu: justice aimed at restoring broken relationships rather than only punishing. The TRC remains contested; many victims felt that truth without prosecutions or adequate reparations was too little.

The **restorative justice** movement worldwide, with its victim-offender meetings and community conferences, shares this relational logic, though its main roots lie elsewhere, including in Indigenous practices in New Zealand and North America.

More recently, ubuntu has entered debates about artificial intelligence. In a 2020 paper for Harvard's Carr Center, the researcher Sabelo Mhlambi argued that much AI ethics rests on an individualist model of the person as a rational, autonomous chooser, and proposed ubuntu's relational personhood as an alternative foundation. On this view, the wrongs of surveillance and algorithmic discrimination are not only violations of individual rights but damage to the relationships and communities through which people become who they are.

The connection is illuminating but needs care. Gyekye's worry applies: a relational ethic must still protect individuals from their communities, and a government can invoke 'harmony' to silence dissent. The challenge, in courtrooms and in code, is to honour relationships without dissolving the individual.

vocabulary.definition: A southern African ethical and metaphysical idea that a person is a person through other persons; humanness achieved in community.
vocabulary.example: Desmond Tutu appealed to ubuntu to defend a justice aimed at restoring relationships.

vocabulary.definition: Hountondji's critical label for presenting a people's collective customs, myths and proverbs as a unanimous philosophy.
vocabulary.example: Tempels's Bantu Philosophy is the classic target of the critique of ethnophilosophy.

vocabulary.definition: Oruka's term for critical, reasoned reflection by individual sages within traditional communities, as opposed to merely transmitted folk wisdom.
vocabulary.example: A sage who gives reasons for rejecting a local belief in witchcraft displays philosophic sagacity.

vocabulary.definition: Gyekye's view that community deeply shapes persons, but that individuals also have intrinsic worth and rights the community must respect.
vocabulary.example: A moderate communitarian can say a community's custom is unjust to an individual.

vocabulary.definition: Wiredu's programme of critically examining concepts inherited through colonial languages and education, often by testing them in African languages.
vocabulary.example: Trying to state the Cartesian cogito in Akan was Wiredu's model of conceptual decolonization.

vocabulary.definition: In Maffie's reading of Nahua philosophy, the single sacred, ever-moving, self-generating energy of which all things are aspects.
vocabulary.example: Because everything is teotl in motion, Nahua metaphysics is a process monism.

vocabulary.definition: Nahua 'truth' understood as well-rootedness or authenticity in teotl, rather than as correspondence to fact.
vocabulary.example: A person living a balanced life on the slippery earth could be called true in the sense of neltiliztli.

vocabulary.definition: Dussel's term for Europe's story that modernity arose from internal resources alone, concealing the role of conquest and justifying violence as civilising.
vocabulary.example: Dussel's phrase ego conquiro challenges the myth of modernity by placing 1492 before Descartes.

thinkingExercise.title: Who Made You a Person?
thinkingExercise.prompt: Test the communitarian and liberation ideas against your own life and education.
steps: List five relationships or communities without which you would not be recognisably who you are. For each, say what it gave you that you could not have given yourself.
Decide between Menkiti and Gyekye: is there anything about your worth or rights that does not depend on those relationships? Give a concrete case where community and individual conflicted.

Try Wiredu's test: pick a philosophical concept from this course (for instance 'mind', 'self' or 'truth') and ask how it would be expressed in another language you know, or how a speaker of another language might misunderstand it. What changes?
Apply Dussel: name one story about progress or history you were taught in school. Whose perspective was it told from, and what would it look like told from the side of those it affected?

summary: Hountondji criticised 'ethnophilosophy' as unanimist; Oruka's sage philosophy showed individual critical reflection among unschooled elders.

Ubuntu holds that a person is a person through other persons; Menkiti saw personhood as achieved, Gyekye defended a moderate view with individual rights, and Metz framed ubuntu as a theory of harmonious relationship.
Wiredu's conceptual decolonization tests inherited concepts in African languages, questioning the cogito and mind-body dualism, and he proposed consensus democracy.
Maffie reconstructs Nahua philosophy as a process monism of teotl, with truth as well-rootedness (neltiliztli) and ethics as balance on slippery earth.
Dussel argues modernity began with the conquest of 1492 (ego conquiro before ego cogito) and that philosophy should start from the excluded Other.
Comparative philosophy must avoid both romanticising and flattening: these traditions are claims to be taken seriously and argued with.

quiz.question: What was Hountondji's main objection to ethnophilosophy?
options: It was written in African languages
It presented a whole people as sharing one unanimous worldview, neglecting individual critical thinkers
It relied too heavily on formal logic
quiz.explanation: Hountondji called this 'unanimism': real philosophy involves individuals who argue and disagree.

quiz.question: Oruka distinguished the philosophic sage from the folk sage because the philosophic sage:
options: Reflects critically on received wisdom and may reject it with reasons
quiz.explanation: The philosophic sage goes beyond transmitting tradition to reasoned critical reflection on it.

quiz.question: Menkiti argued that personhood in much African thought is something achieved through moral development in community.
quiz.explanation: Menkiti described personhood as processual and normative, fully achieved by elders who have lived well.

quiz.question: A village council insists a young woman must accept an arranged marriage for the sake of communal harmony. Which thinker's view gives the clearest basis for criticising the council?
quiz.explanation: Gyekye insisted individuals have intrinsic worth and rights the community must respect, allowing criticism of communal decisions.

quiz.question: Why did Wiredu think 'I think, therefore I am' loses force in Akan?
options: Akan has no word for thinking
In Akan, existence is expressed as being there at some place, so a placeless mind is hard to state
quiz.explanation: Since 'to be' is expressed locatively (wo ho), the cogito becomes 'I am there, somewhere', undermining the idea of a non-spatial mind.

quiz.question: In Maffie's reading, what is teotl?
options: The Nahua word for the soul
A single sacred, self-generating energy in constant motion, of which everything is an aspect
quiz.explanation: Maffie interprets teotl as a process monism, not a personal deity.

quiz.question: In Nahua thought as Maffie reconstructs it, truth is primarily correspondence between statements and facts.
quiz.explanation: Truth as neltiliztli is well-rootedness or authenticity; persons and actions can be true in this sense.

quiz.question: Dussel's phrase 'ego conquiro' is meant to suggest that:
options: European modern selfhood was shaped by conquest, which preceded and underpinned the 'ego cogito'
quiz.explanation: Dussel dates modernity to 1492 and argues European self-centredness grew from conquest.

quiz.question: Which of these best describes the danger of 'flattening' non-Western traditions?
options: Translating them into familiar Western categories, such as calling ubuntu 'just communitarianism'
Reading them in translation at all
quiz.explanation: Flattening forces distinctive ideas into borrowed boxes and loses what is new in them; argument and careful comparison are encouraged.

quiz.question: South Africa's Constitutional Court invoked ubuntu when abolishing the death penalty in S v Makwanyane (1995).
quiz.explanation: Several judges appealed to ubuntu's respect for the dignity of every person, including offenders.

goDeeper.body:
The debate over personhood in African philosophy has become one of the most active in contemporary ethics. Menkiti's view raises sharp questions about moral status: if young children are not yet persons in the thick sense, what do we owe them? Defenders reply that Menkiti's 'personhood' is an honorific notion, like 'a real mensch', and does not deny children moral protection. Others, such as Polycarp Ikuenobe in *Philosophical Perspectives on Communalism and Morality in African Traditions* (2006), defend a sophisticated normative account. Thaddeus Metz's *A Relational Moral Theory* (2022) develops ubuntu-inspired ethics into a full rival to utilitarianism and Kantianism and applies it to topics like bioethics and the moral status of animals.

In Nahua studies, Maffie's reading has been challenged. Some historians think it imposes a unified philosophical system on sources that are fragmentary and filtered through Spanish friars. Others question whether 'monism' is the right Western term at all, since applying it risks the flattening Maffie warns against. Sebastian Purcell has developed a virtue-ethical reading of Nahua thought, focused on rootedness and the good life on slippery earth.

Latin American thought also includes debates Dussel only partly represents. The Peruvian sociologist Aníbal Quijano introduced the concept of the **coloniality of power** (around 1990–2000): colonial hierarchies of race and labour persisted after formal independence. Walter Mignolo developed this into a broader decolonial programme. Critics within Latin America, however, warn that decolonial theory can romanticise indigenous traditions and dismiss science and liberal rights as merely European. These internal debates are themselves a sign of a living philosophical tradition.

readings.note: His early, influential essays, including the critique of tradition and the case for conceptual analysis.

readings.note: Includes the methodology and the interviews themselves.

readings.author: James Maffie
readings.note: Long and detailed; chapters 1 and 3 give the core metaphysics.

readings.title: Philosophy of Liberation
readings.author: Enrique Dussel
readings.note: A dense but short programmatic statement; read the opening chapter on history and geopolitics.

questions: Can a relational account of personhood protect dissenters and minorities as well as a rights-based individualism can?
Is it possible to reconstruct a pre-conquest philosophy from sources written by its conquerors? What standards should such reconstruction meet?
Does Dussel's account of 1492 change how you understand Descartes, or is it a different subject altogether?
